title: Those who work and those who post
gist: Yglesias argues the key political divide is not moderates vs. progressives but executives accountable for outcomes vs. backbench legislators who mostly 'post'; Mamdani governs pragmatically as NYC mayor in service of leftist power-building, as Bernie Sanders did in Burlington. He urges moderate Democrats not to panic about a leftist 2028 nominee because governing constraints force pragmatism.

insights.claim: Politicians in executive roles with real accountability for outcomes tend to govern pragmatically, while safe-seat backbench legislators can build careers on taking positions without setting priorities.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Expect executives (mayors, governors, presidents) to be more market- and business-climate-sensitive than their legislative rhetoric suggests.
insights.quote: There’s a kind of objective incentive for a mayor or a governor or a president to try to be responsible, while many legislators can get away with just posting.
insights.locator: Posting versus governing

insights.claim: Yglesias argues the under-discussed political divide in the US is between officeholders with executive accountability and backbench legislators, rather than between moderates and progressives.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Factional labels are a weak predictor of policy outcomes; office type matters more.
insights.locator: Which is all just to say

insights.claim: The natural state of a safe-seat Democratic legislator is to say yes to many interest-group asks without considering whether they are contradictory, assuming someone else will choose what actually happens.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Legislative endorsements of expansive agendas overstate what will actually be enacted.
insights.locator: The difference is that the natural

insights.claim: Yglesias claims actual governing tends to produce consensus, whereas factionalism among 'posters' becomes intense.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Policy convergence is likelier once candidates reach executive office than campaign rhetoric implies.
insights.quote: Actual governing, though, tends to produce consensus instead.
insights.locator: As a professional poster myself

insights.claim: The practical need to count votes and make deals pushes legislators who engage in governing to think harder, as Sheldon Whitehouse did in negotiating a bipartisan energy permitting bill.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Bipartisan permitting reform is a live legislative effort with engaged dealmakers.
insights.locator: Legislators, after all, can accept

insights.claim: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani governs pragmatically not because he is a moderate but because doing a good job as mayor is the best way to build leftist political power.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Lower tail risk of disruptive policy in NYC than Mamdani's ideology implied at election.
insights.locator: The reason a hardcore leftist

insights.claim: Bernie Sanders as mayor of Burlington delivered cost-effective city services, safe streets, and economic development rather than socialism, and is the closest precedent for Mamdani's governance.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Historical precedent suggests left mayors can be fiscally ordinary in practice.
insights.locator: The clearest precedent I can think

insights.claim: Mamdani does not want Wall Street firms to close NYC offices and relocate jobs to New Jersey or Texas, according to Yglesias.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Reduces perceived risk of anti-finance policy driving NYC financial-sector flight.
insights.quote: Mamdani doesn’t want Wall Street firms to close their New York City offices and send those jobs to New Jersey or Texas.

insights.claim: Mamdani refused City Council pressure to give public-school paraprofessionals a bonus and successfully fought to delay a state-mandated class-size reduction he had voted for as a legislator.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Signals NYC fiscal discipline against labor-group spending asks.
insights.locator: Mamdani is more left-wing than Biden

insights.claim: Mamdani has shifted from a free-bus pledge to focusing on speeding up buses because free buses would be costly and not very beneficial.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: NYC transit spending prioritizes service speed over fare elimination, preserving budget room.
insights.locator: He ran on making the bus free

insights.claim: New York City remains a high-tax, high-spend jurisdiction and Mamdani is working to raise spending further, but he is concentrating fiscal capacity on expanding child care.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Watch child care expansion as NYC's main new fiscal commitment; spending direction is still up.
insights.locator: He hasn’t reinvented himself

insights.claim: Mamdani declined activists' push to fight the NYPD police commissioner because a good relationship with the governor builds more power and there is no actual problem with the NYPD status quo.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Suggests continuity in NYC public-safety policy.
insights.locator: Activists want him to pick a fight

insights.claim: Mamdani's ideological content is similar to Bill de Blasio's, but de Blasio was a weak figure who governed by parceling out interest-group 'slop', while Mamdani has more leverage to insist on his priorities.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Leadership strength, not ideology, determines whether city policy is coherent.
insights.locator: The ideological content of Mamdani

insights.claim: Chicago under Brandon Johnson is the counterexample of a left mayor floundering and discrediting the left.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Chicago governance seen as a cautionary case for municipal fiscal/policy risk.
insights.locator: The alternative, on display

insights.claim: Former governors Maggie Hassan, Jeanne Shaheen, and John Hickenlooper governed as pragmatic moderates but as senators endorsed the expansive multi-trillion Build Back Better.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Same politicians shift positions depending on accountability; discount legislative rhetoric.
insights.locator: The reverse-Mamdanis of the U.S. Congress

insights.claim: New Hampshire kept no tax on earned income under governors Hassan and Shaheen, and Hickenlooper declined to back a 2011 Colorado income and sales tax increase for schools.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Executive office constrains tax hikes even among Democrats.
insights.locator: New Hampshire, notably

insights.claim: As Virginia governor, Abigail Spanberger said she would not repeal right-to-work and is fighting the legislature over a public-sector bargaining bill she thinks would hurt local government finances.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Virginia business climate and labor rules likely stable under Democratic governor.
insights.locator: Or look at someone like Abigail Spanberger

insights.claim: Democratic governors Kathy Hochul and Maura Healey are pushing for new natural-gas pipelines because of concerns about state energy prices.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Northeast pipeline buildout gains political support from Democratic executives on affordability grounds - relevant to midstream gas.
insights.quote: Kathy Hochul and Maura Healey, neither of whom are particularly moderate as a question of factional identification, are both trying to get new natural-gas pipelines built

insights.claim: Governors and mayors must brag about outcomes in their jurisdiction, while legislators can brag merely about positions taken.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Energy prices and affordability outcomes drive executive policy more than ideology.
insights.locator: The basic difference is that

insights.claim: Biden behaved like a 'President Senator', declining to set priorities, so no one on his team was empowered to make pro-affordability decisions that crossed labor unions or environmental groups.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Explains past administration energy/affordability policy inconsistencies.
insights.locator: President Senator vs. the strong mayor

insights.claim: The Biden team weighed the economic impact of international oil sanctions because green groups did not lobby on them, but did not apply that logic to Interior Department drilling fees, which those groups did lobby on.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Interest-group lobbying, not consistent economics, shaped federal oil and drilling policy.
insights.locator: They could care about the economic impact

insights.claim: Yglesias argues moderates have much to like in non-moderate Mamdani and much to dislike in self-identified moderate Biden because executive strength matters more than ideology.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Evaluate leaders on priority-setting capacity rather than label.

insights.claim: Yglesias urges moderate Democrats not to rally behind establishment figures like Gavin Newsom or Kamala Harris merely to block a leftist from winning the 2028 primary.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Leftist 2028 nominee scenario may carry less policy-tail risk than feared.
insights.locator: For 2028, I really want moderate Democrats

insights.claim: Yglesias predicts a hypothetical President Ocasio-Cortez in 2029 would not spend heavy political capital on ICE abolition or overhaul the entire $5 trillion-a-year health system at once.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Health-care sector disruption risk from a left president is likely incremental, not wholesale.
insights.quote: She’s also not going to overhaul the entire $5 trillion-a-year health-care system in one fell swoop any more than President Newsom would.

insights.claim: Slogans like 'abolish ICE' or free health care for everyone are takes rather than governing plans, as they ignore priorities, budget limits, and recalcitrant legislators.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Discount maximalist campaign slogans when modeling policy outcomes.
insights.locator: A lot of what passes for factional

insights.claim: Yglesias' ideal 2028 outcome is a smart moderate campaign critiquing the Democratic establishment, preferred over Ro Khanna or Ocasio-Cortez.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Signals center-left appetite for an anti-establishment moderate candidate.
insights.locator: My ideal 2028 outcome

insights.claim: Yglesias personally favors a revenue-neutral carbon tax set at the global social cost of carbon with revenue offsetting payroll taxes, while acknowledging it will not happen.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Carbon tax remains politically non-viable in the author's view.
insights.locator: But I have all kinds of takes
